title: WHAT IF THE VOICE YOU'VE BEEN CALLING “BIBLICAL” IS ONLY THE VOICE YOU'VE HEARD ALL YOUR LIFE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE VOICE YOU'VE BEEN CALLING “BIBLICAL” IS ONLY THE VOICE YOU'VE HEARD ALL YOUR LIFE?

The Terrifying Difference Between Knowing Christian Language and Knowing Christ—And Why an Entire Generation Could Be Learning to Recognize the Sound of Truth Without Ever Learning to Discern Truth Itself.

There is something deeply unsettling about the possibility that you could spend twenty years inside a church, memorize hundreds of Bible verses, recognize every worship song, understand when to shout “Amen,” and still be unable to recognize when someone is twisting the Word of God right in front of you.
Not because you're unintelligent.
Not because you don't love Jesus.
But because somewhere along the way, you may have been taught to recognize what Christianity sounds like more than you've been taught to recognize what Scripture actually says.
And the most frightening part?
A lie doesn't always arrive sounding like a lie.
Sometimes it comes wrapped in a Bible verse.
Sometimes it comes from a pulpit you've trusted for years.
Sometimes it sounds so much like the Christianity you grew up with that questioning it feels almost like questioning God Himself.
But what if the thing you're afraid to question isn't God?
What if it's simply something people taught you about Him?
And what if the difference between those two things is far more important than you've ever imagined?
Because Jesus never commanded us to believe something merely because it sounds religious.
He called us to follow Him.
And those are not always the same thing.
Imagine a young woman sitting in the back row of a church.
We'll call her Sarah.

She's been attending services since childhood. Her parents taught Sunday school. She knows the songs. She knows the language. She knows when to stand, when to bow her head, when to raise her hands, and which answers people expect when someone asks how she's doing spiritually.
“Blessed.”
“Highly favored.”
“God is good.”
And she means it.
At least she wants to.
But privately, Sarah has questions she doesn't know how to ask.
She's heard that real Christians never struggle with doubt.
She's heard that if she has enough faith, God will always remove her suffering.
She's heard that questioning a spiritual leader is rebellion.
She's heard that financial prosperity is proof of God's favor.
She's heard that if she gives enough, prays enough, serves enough, and believes hard enough, God will finally be pleased with her.
And whenever something doesn't make sense, someone tells her the same thing.
“Just have faith.”
So she stops asking.
She learns to smile while confused.
She learns to say “Amen” when she's uncertain.
She learns to mistake silence for submission.
Until one night, alone with an open Bible, she reads something that unsettles everything.
Jesus is not speaking like some of the people who claim to represent Him.
He welcomes the weary.
He confronts religious hypocrisy.
He rebukes those who burden others without lifting a finger to help.
He warns about false prophets.
He tells His followers to recognize people by their fruit.
And suddenly Sarah finds herself staring at the pages, whispering a question she has been afraid to ask for years.
“Lord… have I been following You, or have I just been following what people told me You were like?”
That question could change a life.
It could also change a church.
Because there is a difference between being familiar with Christian vocabulary and being formed by biblical truth.
And Jesus confronted that difference long before social media, celebrity preachers, viral sermons, or religious algorithms ever existed.
In Matthew 15:8–9, Jesus quotes the prophet Isaiah:

“This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me. But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” — Matthew 15:8–9, KJV
Read that again.
Their mouths were religious.
Their words were reverent.
Their worship was visible.
But their hearts were far away.

Jesus wasn't condemning reverence, worship, or faithful tradition simply because they were familiar. He was exposing something far more dangerous: human commandments being elevated to the authority of God.
In the Greek text of Matthew 15:9, the phrase ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων (entalmata anthrōpōn) means “commandments of men” or “human commands.”
That's the problem.
Not every religious tradition is evil.
Not every familiar phrase is false.
Not every pastor who uses language you've heard before is misleading you.

But when human expectations become untouchable, when inherited opinions are treated as divine commands, and when people are pressured to obey teachings that cannot withstand honest examination under Scripture, something has gone terribly wrong.
We have stopped asking, “Is this what God has said?”
And started asking, “Does this sound like what Christians usually say?”
Those questions can produce very different answers.
And perhaps the clearest example of why this matters appears at the very beginning of Jesus' public ministry.
In Matthew 4, Satan tempts Jesus in the wilderness.
The first temptation concerns hunger.
Jesus has fasted forty days and forty nights.
He is hungry.
Physically weak.
Alone in the wilderness.
The tempter approaches Him with an invitation to turn stones into bread.
Jesus answers with Scripture.
“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.” — Matthew 4:4, KJV
But then something astonishing happens.
In the next temptation, Satan himself quotes Scripture.
Yes.
The devil quotes the Bible.
He takes Jesus to the pinnacle of the temple and urges Him to throw Himself down, citing God's promise of angelic protection from Psalm 91.
Think about that.
The words being quoted were from Scripture.
The source was sacred.
But the proposed application was wicked.
Satan was using a genuine biblical promise to encourage Jesus to put God to the test.
And Jesus answered with another Scripture:
“Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” — Matthew 4:7, KJV
That moment should permanently change how we listen to religious teaching.
A Bible verse can be quoted accurately and still be used to support a false conclusion.
A statement can contain Scripture without faithfully communicating Scripture.
A message can sound powerful while mishandling the very Word it claims to honor.
Jesus did not reject Psalm 91.
He rejected its misuse.
He understood that one passage must not be twisted to contradict another, and that God's promises are not permission to manipulate Him.
So when someone tells you that a teaching must be true because it contains Bible verses, remember the wilderness.
The question is not merely whether Scripture was quoted.
The question is whether Scripture was understood and applied faithfully.
That distinction is not a minor theological technicality.
It can determine whether someone is being led toward the freedom of Christ or deeper into spiritual bondage.
Consider the person who has been told that every illness proves a lack of faith.
Imagine how that teaching lands on a mother sitting beside her sick child.
She has prayed.
She has fasted.
She has cried herself to sleep.
She believes God can heal.
But her child is still suffering.
Now imagine someone tells her that the reason her child hasn't recovered is that she hasn't believed strongly enough.
Do you understand what that can do to a human soul?
She is already carrying grief.
Now she carries guilt.
She is already exhausted.
Now she wonders whether God is disappointed in her.
But Scripture gives us a fuller picture.
Paul pleaded three times for his thorn in the flesh to be removed, and the Lord answered:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Paul's experience does not mean God never heals.
It means ongoing suffering cannot automatically be treated as evidence of spiritual failure.
The Bible teaches us to pray, trust, endure, seek help, and depend on God's grace.
It does not give us permission to shame every suffering believer as though their pain proves defective faith.
And when we teach people otherwise, we may be adding burdens Jesus never commanded them to carry.
Now consider the struggling father who gives an offering while desperately hoping God will rescue his family financially.
He loves Jesus.
He wants to be generous.
But someone has convinced him that giving money guarantees a financial breakthrough.
He gives what he cannot afford because he's afraid withholding it will mean withholding his faith.
Then the breakthrough doesn't come.
His bills remain.
His children still need food.
And he begins wondering whether God has abandoned him.
But what does Scripture actually teach?
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
The Greek word ἀνάγκης (anankēs), translated “necessity” in the KJV, carries the sense of compulsion or constraint.
Paul is teaching willing generosity, not coerced giving.
And that matters.
Because a church should never need to manipulate someone's fear in order to inspire generosity.
Biblical giving is an act of worship and love, not a payment to purchase God's favor.
Grace is not for sale.
God is not a vending machine.
And Jesus Christ did not shed His blood so frightened people could be convinced that their next financial blessing depends on buying divine approval.
He came to redeem sinners.
He came to reconcile us to the Father.
He came to give Himself for people who could never purchase their own salvation.
That is the Gospel.
And whenever religious language obscures that Gospel, we must be willing to examine what we're hearing.
But perhaps someone reading this is beginning to feel uncomfortable.
Because you've repeated some of those teachings.
You've shared sermons without checking the passages.
You've defended statements because they came from someone you respected.
You've called something “biblical” because it sounded like the Christianity you grew up hearing.
Maybe you've even corrected other people with verses you never studied in context.
And now you're wondering whether you've been part of the problem.
Please hear this.
The purpose of discernment is not to produce a generation of angry Christians who distrust everyone.
It is to produce disciples who love Jesus enough to care about what He actually said.
You do not need to become cynical to become discerning.
You do not need to mock the church to examine a teaching.
You do not need to despise your pastor to open your Bible.
And you certainly do not need to pretend you've understood everything.
In fact, one of the most beautiful examples of biblical discernment comes from believers who were willing to listen carefully while checking the Scriptures.
Acts 17:11 describes the Jews in Berea who received Paul's message eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily to determine whether what he said was true.
Notice the balance.
They were receptive.
But they were not gullible.
They were eager.
But they were not careless.
They listened to Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, and still examined his message against the Scriptures.
In the Greek text, the word ἀνακρίνοντες (anakrinontes) describes examining, investigating, or scrutinizing.
They weren't searching for excuses to reject the truth.
They were investigating whether the message agreed with God's revealed Word.
And Luke commends them for it.
Imagine what could happen if our churches rediscovered that spirit.
Imagine believers who don't merely ask whether a sermon was emotional, but whether it was faithful.
Imagine young Christians who aren't intimidated when someone says, “The Bible clearly teaches this,” because they know how to open the passage and read what comes before and after it.
Imagine parents teaching their children not only Bible stories but also how to understand what those stories reveal about God.
Imagine small groups where sincere questions aren't treated as threats.
Imagine pastors who can say, “I was wrong about that passage,” without feeling their entire ministry is collapsing.
Imagine congregations where truth matters more than reputation.
Where repentance matters more than image.
Where Scripture is treasured more than charisma.
And where Jesus is more important than the personality delivering the sermon.
Wouldn't that be beautiful?
But there is another danger we must confront.
Because the problem isn't only false teaching coming from someone else.
Sometimes the most familiar religious language we need to question is coming from our own mouths.
“I surrender everything to God.”
Do we?
“Jesus is Lord.”
Does His authority shape our private decisions?
“I forgive because Christ forgave me.”
Have we released the bitterness we've been feeding for years?
“I trust God's timing.”
Or do we trust Him only when His timing agrees with ours?
“I love my neighbor.”
Including the person who embarrassed us?
Including the family member who wounded us?
Including the believer who disagrees with us?
It's possible to use beautiful Christian words while resisting the very truth those words express.
And Jesus addressed that too.
In Luke 6:46, He asks:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — KJV
That question doesn't merely confront bad theology.
It confronts divided hearts.
Because biblical truth is not something we are called only to identify.
We are called to believe it, submit to it, and live in response to it.
James 1:22 warns us to be doers of the Word, not hearers only, deceiving ourselves.
A person can win an argument about doctrine and still refuse to love their neighbor.
A person can identify a false teacher and still cherish secret sin.
A person can quote the Greek New Testament and still lack humility.
Knowledge is necessary.
But knowledge alone is not spiritual maturity.
First Corinthians 8:1 reminds us that knowledge can puff up, while love builds up.
And the goal of sound teaching is not simply to create people who are better at correcting others.
It is to form people who know, love, trust, and obey Jesus Christ.
That is where this conversation becomes deeply personal.
Because at some point, every believer must face a question that cannot be answered by applause, church attendance, or familiarity with religious expressions.
Has the truth I know about Jesus actually changed the way I live before Him?
Not perfectly.
None of us can claim that.
But genuinely.
When the Holy Spirit exposes sin, do we repent?
When Scripture challenges our assumptions, do we listen?
When God's Word confronts our pride, do we humble ourselves?
When the Gospel reminds us that salvation is by grace, do we stop trying to earn the love Christ has already demonstrated at the cross?
And when someone asks us a difficult biblical question, do we help them search the Scriptures, or do we silence them because their question makes us uncomfortable?
Perhaps the most dangerous kind of religious familiarity is the kind that makes us feel spiritually safe while leaving us unchanged.
Jesus warned about this in Matthew 7:21–23.
He described people who called Him “Lord, Lord” and pointed to extraordinary religious activities, yet were not truly known by Him.
That passage should sober us.
But it should not drive a sincere, struggling believer into despair.
Jesus was not teaching that salvation belongs to those who perform flawlessly.
He was exposing the tragedy of religious profession without genuine relationship and obedience.
And the answer is not to become obsessed with proving ourselves worthy.
The answer is to come to Christ.
Because the same Jesus who warns against empty profession also welcomes sinners who come to Him.
In John 6:37, He says:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — KJV
What a promise.
The person who has been deceived can come.
The person who has deceived others can repent and come.
The believer who has confused religious performance with genuine discipleship can come.
The exhausted Christian who has spent years trying to look spiritually strong can come.
The skeptic who has seen hypocrisy and wonders whether the Gospel is real can come.
And the person who has just realized that much of what they believed about God may need to be examined can come.
Jesus is not threatened by the truth.
He is the truth.
In John 14:6, He declares:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — KJV
In Greek, the word translated “truth” is ἀλήθεια (alētheia).
In this verse, Jesus is not merely claiming to possess correct information.
He is identifying Himself as the truth, the definitive revelation of the Father and the only way to Him.
Christianity is not ultimately about mastering a collection of religious phrases.
It is about the crucified and risen Son of God.
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who lived in perfect obedience where we have failed.
The One who confronted hypocrisy without abandoning mercy.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners without pretending sin was harmless.
The One who carried our sins in His body on the cross.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One through whom forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life are offered by grace through faith.
This is why the Gospel must remain at the center of discernment.
Without the Gospel, discernment can become arrogance.
Without Scripture, religious passion can become confusion.
Without love, correction can become cruelty.
And without Christ, even the most impressive religious vocabulary becomes empty noise.
But when the Word of God is faithfully understood, when the Spirit works through that Word, and when Jesus remains the center, something beautiful happens.
The deceived can discover truth.
The proud can learn humility.
The wounded can begin healing.
The confused can grow in understanding.
The fearful can learn to rest in grace.
And the person who once knew only the language of Christianity can begin to know the Savior those words were always meant to reveal.
That is the transformation worth pursuing.
And perhaps that is why the story of the Samaritan woman in John 4 is so unforgettable.
She came to a well carrying an ordinary water jar.
But her life was anything but ordinary.
Jesus knew her complicated relational history.
He knew the truth she couldn't hide.
And still, He spoke to her.
He did not flatter her.
He did not ignore the reality of her life.
He brought truth into the conversation.
But He also offered living water.
In the middle of that encounter, the woman raised a religious dispute about the proper place of worship.
The Samaritans worshiped on one mountain.
The Jews worshiped in Jerusalem.
It was a serious question rooted in generations of religious division.
Jesus did not treat all beliefs as equally true. He corrected her understanding and pointed toward the new reality of worship made possible through Him.
Then He said:
“God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” — John 4:24, KJV
In the Greek text, the phrase is ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ (en pneumati kai alētheia)—“in spirit and truth.”
Not performance without truth.
Not religious familiarity without genuine worship.
Not outward correctness divorced from the reality of God.
True worship must correspond to who God is and to the revelation He has given through His Son.
And notice what happens next.
The woman encounters Jesus as the promised Messiah.
She leaves her water jar.
She returns to her town.
And she tells people about Him.
Her past did not become the final word over her life.
Her encounter with Christ became the beginning of a new testimony.
That is the heart of our Gospel Warrior message.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because He calls darkness light.
Not because truth is unimportant.
But because His grace meets sinners in the truth and calls them into a transformed life.
He does not save us by teaching us to disguise our brokenness with better religious vocabulary.
He saves us by His grace, through faith, and begins making us new.
And perhaps someone reading this right now is standing at their own well.
You've learned how to sound like a Christian.
But you're tired of pretending.
You've been afraid to admit your doubts.
You've been wounded by people who spoke God's name while acting in ways that contradicted His Word.
You've heard so many competing voices that you're no longer sure which ones to trust.
And somewhere beneath the confusion, there's a quiet prayer.
“Jesus, I don't want to be deceived. I don't want to deceive myself. I just want to know You.”
That is a prayer worth praying.
Open the Gospels.
Read Jesus' words in context.
Pay attention to whom He is addressing, what questions He is answering, and how His teaching fits within the whole counsel of Scripture.
Read the letters of the apostles.
Learn the difference between a command, a promise, a historical description, a proverb, a parable, and a prophetic passage.
Ask what a biblical author intended to communicate to the original audience before deciding how a passage applies to your own life.
Use trustworthy translations and study resources.

Where original-language insights help, use them carefully. Hebrew and Greek words are not secret codes that automatically unlock hidden meanings unavailable to ordinary Bible readers. Their meanings are understood through grammar, context, and usage, not through dramatic claims about isolated words.
And remember that you do not need to become a scholar before you can begin faithfully reading Scripture.
God's Word is not reserved for an intellectual elite.
The church needs faithful teachers, careful students, humble pastors, and ordinary believers who love the truth.
We need one another.
And when you hear a powerful sermon, don't be ashamed to ask whether the preacher has handled the passage accurately.
When a viral Christian quote moves you, don't assume its emotional impact proves its biblical accuracy.
When someone promises blessings that Scripture has not promised, be careful.
When someone uses God's name to demand unquestioning loyalty to themselves, remember that Christ alone is Lord of the church.
And when a teaching is shown to be wrong, have the courage to change your mind.
Repentance is not humiliation.
It is a gift of grace.
There is no shame in discovering that something you believed was mistaken.
The danger is refusing correction because admitting the truth might cost you your reputation.
We should care more about being faithful to Jesus than about appearing as though we've always been right.
And that brings us to something we desperately need to recover in the body of Christ.
A culture where people are not merely impressed by biblical language.
They are transformed by biblical truth.
A culture where the person who says “I don't understand this passage yet” is encouraged to study, not mocked for ignorance.
A culture where a struggling believer can say “Please pray for me” without being treated as spiritually inferior.
A culture where pastors are respected but not placed above correction.
A culture where giving is generous rather than coerced.
A culture where spiritual gifts are exercised under biblical accountability.
A culture where people can disagree on secondary matters without forgetting that they belong to the same Savior.
A culture where we don't confuse volume with authority, popularity with faithfulness, or emotional intensity with the presence of God.
And a culture where every sermon, testimony, devotional, article, and ministry—including Gospel Warrior—is accountable to Scripture.
Yes.
Including us.
Never believe something simply because Gospel Warrior published it.
Open your Bible.
Examine the passages.
Test the interpretation.
If we ever say something that cannot be supported by Scripture, we should be willing to be corrected.
Because the goal of this ministry is not to make you dependent on our voice.
It is to help you become more deeply rooted in the voice of the Good Shepherd as revealed in His Word.
Jesus said in John 10:27:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — KJV
In context, this is about belonging to Christ and following Him, not about treating every inner impression as a direct revelation from God.
His sheep belong to Him.
He knows them.
And they follow Him.
That is the relationship we want to help nurture.
Not dependence on a platform.
Not admiration for a personality.
Not loyalty to a brand.
But a growing love for Jesus Christ, His Gospel, and His Word.
And if this article has challenged you, don't rush away from the discomfort.
Sit with it.
Ask the Lord to search your heart.
Maybe you've been trusting a familiar phrase more than a carefully understood passage.
Maybe you've allowed disappointment with religious people to push you away from Christ Himself.
Maybe you've been defending a tradition without knowing whether Scripture supports it.
Maybe you've been using biblical knowledge to win arguments while neglecting love.
Or maybe you've been carrying guilt because someone taught you that God's acceptance depends on your religious performance.
Whatever the truth exposes, bring it to Jesus.
He does not call us into the light so we can remain condemned beneath the weight of our sin.
He calls us to repentance, faith, forgiveness, and newness of life.
First John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
Do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit's work of exposing sin is not an invitation to run away from Christ.
It is a reason to turn toward Him.
The cross is sufficient.
The risen Savior is alive.
And the grace that forgives also teaches us to walk in a new way.
So here's a question I want you to answer—not for an algorithm, not to impress other Christians, but because someone else may need the honesty of your testimony.
Have you ever discovered that something you believed for years sounded Christian but wasn't actually what the Bible taught?
If you're comfortable, share what changed when you examined Scripture for yourself.
Or simply comment, “Lord, teach me Your truth.”
You do not need to share private details to be welcomed into this conversation.
And if you've been learning to distinguish the voice of Scripture from the noise of religious performance, tell us what God has been teaching you.
Your testimony may help another believer find the courage to open their Bible again.
Your honest question may encourage someone who has been afraid to ask theirs.
Your willingness to admit that you're still learning may remind a struggling Christian that spiritual growth is a journey of grace.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
Not because everyone who reads it will agree.
Not because sharing a post proves your devotion to God.
But because someone in your circle may be quietly struggling with the very questions we've explored.
Someone may have been hurt by distorted teaching.
Someone may be confusing spiritual pressure with God's voice.
Someone may be drifting away from church because they've never been shown the difference between human hypocrisy and the beauty of Christ.
Someone may simply need permission to read the Bible carefully and ask sincere questions.
Invite your family, your friends, those who are spiritually exhausted, those who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still searching for reasons to believe.
Not to pressure them.
But to welcome them into a conversation where Jesus and His Word matter more than appearances.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are meant to help believers go beyond inspirational quotes and grow in their understanding of Scripture, prayer, discipleship, biblical truth, and Christian living.
Because the answer to spiritual confusion is not merely another emotional post.
It is sustained formation in the truth of God's Word.
And that takes time.
It takes teaching.
It takes careful study.
It takes faithful encouragement.
It takes people who are willing to help make sound biblical resources accessible to others.
It is a voluntary act of partnership that can help sustain and expand this work.

It can help us continue developing biblical articles, devotional materials, teaching resources, and discipleship content while making free resources available to people who may not have the means to purchase them.
But I want to be careful about something, especially after everything we've just discussed.

Christians differ in how they understand the application of Old Testament tithing under the new covenant. What is clear in the New Testament is the call to generous, willing, responsible giving, without manipulation or compulsion.

Scripture affirms that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and Paul expresses gratitude for believers who partnered with him through their gifts (Philippians 4:15–18).
You can glorify God through prayer, obedience, service, generosity, faithfulness, sharing truth, and countless acts of love.
These products are simply another way to encourage faith, start meaningful conversations, and help sustain the ministry.
Because our deepest desire is not to build a community that knows how to repeat our words.
It is to serve a community that knows how to examine God's Word.
A community where Christians are equipped to recognize the Gospel, resist deception, grow in holiness, and extend the grace of Christ to a hurting world.
A community that understands why truth matters.
Why context matters.
Why repentance matters.
Why love matters.
And why Jesus must always remain at the center.
One day, the sermons we applauded will be forgotten.
The social media trends we followed will disappear.
The religious arguments we thought were so important may barely matter.
The applause will fade.
The platforms will change.
The familiar voices may fall silent.
But the Word of the Lord endures forever.
And the question that will matter is not how many Christian phrases we memorized or how convincingly we sounded religious.
It is whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
Whether we trusted His Gospel.
Whether we received His grace.
Whether His truth was taking root in our lives.
Whether we were willing to follow Him even when His Word challenged the assumptions we had carried for years.
So don't settle for merely recognizing the sound of Christianity.
Learn the Scriptures.
Test what you hear.
Hold fast to what is good.
Repent when you are wrong.
Love people enough to speak truth with humility.
And above all, come to Jesus Christ—not merely to the language surrounding Him.
Because the tragedy would not be discovering that something you were taught was wrong.
The tragedy would be refusing to open your Bible because the familiar lie felt safer than the transforming truth.
You can spend your whole life recognizing the language of the Shepherd and still miss the invitation to follow Him.
